<!-- theoremx-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro}
For $n \geq 3$ and a prime $p > 0$, 
\begin{align*}
    {\text{NL}}{\left(n,p\right)} = \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}^n \cap \bigcup_{e\geq 1}\bigcup_{\mathbf{b}\in \Gamma_n} \left( B_{r_{p^e}}^+(p^e\mathbf{1}) + p^e\mathbf{b} \right).
\end{align*}
<!-- end theoremx-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:translated_equiv}
We have that $\mathbf{b} \in \Gamma_n$ if and only if there exists a non-negative integer $d$ and pairs of integers $1 \leq u_j < v_j \leq n$ for $1 \leq j \leq d$ so that
\begin{align*}
    \mathbf{b} = \sum_{j=1}^d (\mathbf{e}_{u_j} + \mathbf{e}_{v_j})
\end{align*}
where $\mathbf{e}_{k}$ denotes the $k$-th standard basis vector of $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^n$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The proof of the forward direction is by induction on $|| \mathbf{b} ||_1$. For the inductive step, we subtract $1$ from the largest positive coordinates and show that this vector belongs to $\Gamma_n$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:equiv_char}
We have that
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- rem-1: body_md -->
Let $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{Z}^n_{\geq 2}$. If $\mathbf{c} \in \mathscr{B}_q$, then
\begin{align*}
    \sigma := \sum_{i=1}^n(c_i -1) \geq 2q-1.
\end{align*}
Equivalently, if $\mathbf{c} \in \mathscr{B}_q$, then $q \leq \frac{\sigma+1}{2}$. For a fixed vector $\mathbf{c}$, determining whether $\mathbf{c} \in {\text{NL}}{\left(n,p\right)}$ becomes a finite check. This same bound appears in {\cite[equation (1.6)]{KMRR2026Lefschetz}}.
<!-- end rem-1 -->
<!-- ex-1: body_md -->
Let $n = 3$, $p = q = 3$, and $\mathbf{b} = (4,4,4) \in \Gamma_n$. Then, $r_3 = 1$, and we obtain that the following translate of the taxicab lattice ball centered at 
\begin{align*}
    q\mathbf{1} + q\mathbf{b} = (15,15,15)
\end{align*}
is contained in the non-Lefschetz locus of exponent vectors,
\begin{align*}
    \{ \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq2}^3 : \left \lvert c_1-15 \right\rvert+\left \lvert c_2-15 \right\rvert+\left \lvert c_3-15 \right\rvert  \leq 1\} \subseteq {\text{NL}}{\left(3,3\right)}.
\end{align*}
In particular, $(14,15,15)$ lies on the boundary of the above ball, and we have that
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{F}_3[x,y,z]/(x^{14},y^{15},z^{15})
\end{align*}
fails the WLP. Figure~\ref{fig:NL33} depicts the subset of ${\text{NL}}{\left(3,3\right)}$ with $2 \leq c_i \leq 16$.
<!-- end ex-1 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:HF_ineq}
Let $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ be non-negative integers satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i = 2d$ for some non-negative integer $d$, and
    \item $b_i \leq d$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$.
\end{enumerate}
If 
\begin{align*}
    \prod_{i=1}^n P_{b_i}(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{2d} h_i t^i
\end{align*}
and $h_{-1} := 0$, then $h_d > h_{d-1}$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
When $d = 0$, $h_0 = 1 > 0 = h_{-1}$. Hence we reduce to the case that $d \geq 1$. Without loss of generality, we may suppose that $b_1 \geq \cdots \geq b_n \geq 0$. Let $P$ be the product of chains poset $[b_1] \times \cdots \times [b_n]$. The number of elements of $P$ of rank $i$ is given by $h_i$. We have
\begin{align*}
    b_1 \leq d < d+1 \leq \left( \sum_{i=2}^n b_i\right)+1.
\end{align*}
Hence, Dhand's strict unimodality criterion for products of chains {\cite[Lemma 2.1(3)]{Dhand2014}} implies that $h_d > h_{d-1}$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $\mathbf{c} \in \mathscr{B}_q$. Then, $\mathbf{c} = q(\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{b})+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$ as in \eqref{eq:descr_Bq}. Let $S = \mathbb{K}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ and $J := (x_1^{b_1+1},\ldots,x_n^{b_n+1})$. The Hilbert series of $S/J$ is given by $\prod_{i=1}^{n} P_{b_i}(t)$, and the socle degree of $S/J$ is $\sum_{i=1}^{n} b_i = 2d$ for some non-negative integer $d$. By Lemma \ref{lem:HF_ineq} together with symmetry of the Hilbert function, we have that 
\begin{align*}
    \dim_{\mathbb{K}} [S/J]_d > \dim_{\mathbb{K}} [S/J]_{d+1}.
\end{align*}
Thus, there exists $f \in [S]_d$ satisfying $f \notin J$ and $Lf \in J$ where $L = x_1+\cdots+x_n$.

For $1 \leq i \leq n$, put $\varepsilon^+_i := \max\{0,\varepsilon_i\}$ and $\varepsilon_i^- := \min\{0,\varepsilon_i\}$. Then, $\varepsilon_i = \varepsilon_i^+ + \varepsilon_i^-$ and $|| \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} ||_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n (\varepsilon_i^+ - \varepsilon_i^-)$. Let $I := (x_1^{c_1},\ldots,x_n^{c_n})$, and put $\mu := f^q x_1^{\varepsilon_1^+}\cdots x_n^{\varepsilon_n^+}$. We will show that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mu \notin I$,
    \item $L^q\mu \in I$,
    \item $\deg(L^{q-1}\mu) \leq \lfloor \frac{\sigma -1}{2} \rfloor$ where $\sigma$ denotes the socle degree of $S/I$.
\end{enumerate}
Items (1) and (2) imply that there exists $0\leq s \leq q-1$ such that $L^s\mu \notin I$ and $L^{s+1}\mu \in I$. Hence $L^s\mu$ is in the kernel of the multiplication map of $L$ on $S/I$. Item (3) implies that this kernel element has degree less than half the socle degree. For an Artinian quotient by a monomial ideal, verifying the WLP is equivalent to checking that multiplication by $L$ has maximal rank \cite{harima2003weak}. Thus, $S/I$ fails the WLP.

\textbf{Claim 1}. We show that $\mu \notin I$.

\textit{Proof of Claim 1.} Let $x^{\mathbf{u}}$ be a monomial appearing in the support of $f$ which does not belong to $J$. Then, $0 \leq u_i \leq b_i$ for $1 \leq i \leq n$. The $x_i$-degree of $x^{q\mathbf{u}} x^{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^{+}}$ satisfies
\begin{align*}
    qu_i + \varepsilon_i^+ 
    &\leq qb_i+\varepsilon_i^+ \\
    &= c_i - q - \varepsilon_i^- \\
    &\leq c_i-1.
\end{align*}
Thus, $\mu \notin I$.

\textbf{Claim 2}. We show that $L^q\mu \in I$.

\textit{Proof of Claim 2.} We observe that
\begin{align*}
    L^q\mu = (Lf)^q x^{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^+}.
\end{align*}
Since $Lf \in J$, we have that 
\begin{align*}
    (Lf)^q x^{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^+} \in J^{[q]}\cdot (x^{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}^+}) \subseteq I.
\end{align*}

\textbf{Claim 3}. We show that $\deg(L^{q-1}\mu) \leq \lfloor \frac{\sigma -1}{2} \rfloor$ where $\sigma$ denotes the socle degree of $S/I$.

\textit{Proof of Claim 3.} We compute
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:deg}
    \deg(L^{q-1}\mu) = qd + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \varepsilon_i^+ + q -1.
\end{equation}
We compute 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:socle_deg}
    \sigma = (q-1)n + 2qd + \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^+ + \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^-.
\end{equation}
Using equations \eqref{eq:deg} and \eqref{eq:socle_deg}, we compute
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:eq}
\begin{aligned}
    \sigma -1 -2\deg(L^{q-1}\mu)
    &= (n-2)(q-1)-1 - \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^+ - \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^- \right) \\
    &= r_q - || \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} ||_1 \\
    &\geq 0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The identity in equation \eqref{eqn:eq} explains the taxicab radius in Theorem \ref{thm:intro}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:prime_to_p_centering}
Let $c_1,\ldots,c_n$ be positive integers. If $p\nmid r$ and $\delta_r(-j)$ is a summand of $\delta_{c_1}\cdots\delta_{c_n}$, then
\begin{align*}
    r+2j = \sigma+1
\end{align*}
where $\sigma = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (c_i - 1)$ is the socle degree of $\operatorname{A_\mathbf{c}}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:divisible_by_p}
If $\mathbf{c} \in {\text{NL}}{\left(n,p\right)}$ and $\delta_r(-j)$ is a summand of $\delta_{c_1}\cdots\delta_{c_n}$ so that equation \eqref{eq:failure_of_wlp} holds, then $p \mid r$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Suppose by contradiction that $p\nmid r$. Then, we compute  
\begin{align*}
    \sigma+1 &= r+2j & & \text{(Lemma \ref{lem:prime_to_p_centering})} \\
    &\leq r+2j+(r-1) \\
    &\leq \sigma, & & (\text{equation } \eqref{eq:failure_of_wlp})
\end{align*}
which is a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:iso_M_rho_as_ci}
For $0 \leq \rho_i < \min(c_i,q)$, let $u_i := \lfloor \frac{c_i-1-\rho_i}{q}\rfloor$. Define 
\begin{align*}
    C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}} := \mathbb{K}[y_1,\ldots,y_n]/(y_1^{u_1+1},\ldots,y_n^{u_n+1}).
\end{align*}
Let $Z$ act on $C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ by $Y := y_1+\cdots+y_n$. Then, $C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}} \cong M_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ as $\mathbb{K}[Z]$-modules.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The map $C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}} \rightarrow M_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ sending $y_1^{a_1}\cdots y_n^{a_n}$ to $x_1^{\rho_1+a_1q}\cdots x_n^{\rho_n+a_nq}$ is an isomorphism of $\mathbb{K}[Z]$-modules.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:E_ineq}
For $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $0 \leq \kappa_i \leq q-1$ be such that $c_i-1-\rho_i = q u_i + \kappa_i$. Put $\eta_i := q-1-\kappa_i$ and $E := \sum_{i=1}^n\left( \rho_i + \eta_i \right)$. Then,
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $0 \leq \eta_i \leq q-1$,
    \item $c_i = q(u_i+1) + \rho_i - \eta_i$, and
    \item $|| \mathbf{c}-q(\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{u}) ||_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n \left \lvert \rho_i - \eta_i \right\rvert \leq E$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:descr_E}
Let $\Delta := \sigma - 2(j+q\lambda-1)$. Then, $\Delta \geq 1$ and
\begin{equation}
    E = (n-2)(q-1) -\Delta -q(\lambda-1).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By equation \eqref{eq:failure_of_wlp}, $\Delta \geq 1$. Lemma \ref{lem:E_ineq} implies that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:alt_format_for_sigma}
\begin{aligned}
    \sigma &= \sum_{i=1}^n \left( c_i -1 \right) \\
    &= q \sum_{i=1}^n  u_i  + n(q-1) + \sum_{i=1}^n \rho_i - \sum_{i=1}^n \eta_i.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Substituting equations \eqref{eqn:alt_format_for_sigma} and \eqref{eqn:formula_for_j_zero} into $\Delta =  \sigma - 2(j+q\lambda-1)$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
     \Delta &= \sigma - 2(j+q\lambda-1) \\
     &= q \sum_{i=1}^n u_i  + n(q-1) + \sum_{i=1}^n \rho_i  - \sum_{i=1}^n \eta_i   - 2\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \rho_i  + q j_0 +q\lambda-1 \right) \\
     &= n(q-1) - \sum_{i=1}^n (\rho_i + \eta_i) + q\left( \sum_{i=1}^nu_i -2j_0-2\lambda \right)+2 \\
     &= n(q-1) -E - q(\lambda+1) +2 \quad\quad (\ref{eqn:lam_plus_j_zero}) \\
     &= (n-2)(q-1) -E -q(\lambda-1).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:even}
With notation as in Section 2.2, we have that $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i + \lambda-1$ is even. For $1 \leq k \leq n$, 
\begin{equation}
    2u_k \leq \sum_{i=1}^n u_i + \lambda-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $w \in C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ be a homogeneous generator corresponding to the summand $\delta_\lambda(-j_0)$. From the Jordan decomposition of $C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ as a $\mathbb{K}[Y]$-module, we have that the image of $w$ in $C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}/YC_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ is non-zero. $C_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}/YC_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}$ is a quotient of the algebra
\begin{align*}
    B_k := \frac{\mathbb{K}[y_1,\ldots,\widehat{y_k},\ldots,y_n]}{(y_1^{u_1+1},\ldots,\widehat{y_k^{u_k+1}},\ldots,y_n^{u_n+1})}.
\end{align*}
Hence the degree of $w$ is at most the socle degree of $B_k$, i.e.,
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:bnd}
    j_0 \leq \sum_{i=1}^nu_i - u_k.
\end{equation}
Combining equations \eqref{eq:bnd} and \eqref{eqn:lam_plus_j_zero} implies
\begin{align*}
    2u_k \leq 2 \left( \sum_{i=1}^nu_i - j_0 \right) = \sum_{i=1}^nu_i + \lambda -1,
\end{align*}
and the right-hand side is  even.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:choose_b}
Let $\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^n$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq1}$. Suppose $\sum_{i=1}^n  u_i + \lambda -1$ is even and $2u_j \leq \sum_{i=1}^n  u_i+\lambda-1$ for all $1 \leq j \leq n$. Then, there exists $\mathbf{b} \in \Gamma_n$ so that $0 \leq b_j \leq u_j$ for all $j$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n(u_i-b_i) \leq \lambda -1$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $M = \max_i u_i$. Let $1 \leq k \leq n$ be an integer so that $M = u_k$.

\underline{Case 1.} Suppose that $2 M \leq \sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ is even. Then, $\mathbf{b} := \mathbf{u} \in \Gamma_n$.

\underline{Case 2.} Suppose that $2 M \leq \sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ is odd. Put $b_i := u_i$ for $i \neq k$, and put $b_k := u_k-1$. Since $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ is odd, $M \neq 0$, and hence $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq0}^n$. Next, we have that $2\max_i b_i \leq 2 u_k$. Since $2u_k \leq \sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ (assumption) and $2u_k$ is even and $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ is odd (assumption), the difference in parity implies that
\begin{align*}
    2u_k \leq \sum_{i=1}^n u_i-1 = || \mathbf{b} ||_1.
\end{align*}
Thus, $2\max_i b_i \leq || \mathbf{b} ||_1$. Since in addition $|| \mathbf{b} ||_1$ is even, $\mathbf{b} \in \Gamma_n$ by \eqref{eqn:gamma_n}.

Since $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i + \lambda -1$ is even (assumption) and $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i$ is odd (assumption), it follows that $\lambda-1$ is odd. Hence $\lambda-1 \geq 1$, and it follows that 
\begin{align*}
    || \mathbf{u}-\mathbf{b} ||_1 =1 \leq \lambda-1.
\end{align*}

\underline{Case 3.} Suppose $\sum_{i=1}^nu_i < 2M$. Let $b_i := u_i$ for $i \neq k$ and $b_k := \sum_{i=1}^n u_i-M$. By construction, $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n b_i = 2(\sum_{i=1}^n u_i-M)$. For $j \neq k$, we have
\begin{align*}
    b_j = u_j \leq \sum_{i\neq k} u_i = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i-M = b_k.
\end{align*}
Thus, for $1 \leq j \leq n$, 
\begin{align*}
    2 b_j \leq 2 b_k = 2\left(\sum_{i=1}^n u_i-M\right),
\end{align*}
and it follows that $\mathbf{b} \in \Gamma_n$.

The hypothesis $\sum_{i=1}^n  u_i < 2M$ implies that $b_k \leq u_k$. The hypothesis $2u_k \leq \sum_{i=1}^n u_i + \lambda-1$ implies $2M - \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \leq \lambda-1$. We compute that
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{i=1}^n (u_i - b_i) = 2M - \sum_{i=1}^n  u_i \leq \lambda-1,
\end{align*}
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Continue with the notation of Section 2.2. By Lemmas \ref{lem:even} and \ref{lem:choose_b}, we can find $\mathbf{b} \in \Gamma_n$ so that $0 \leq b_i \leq u_i$ and $|| \mathbf{u}-\mathbf{b} ||_1 \leq \lambda-1$. Put $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} := \mathbf{c}-q(\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{b}).$ We compute
\begin{align*}
    || \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} ||_1 &= || \mathbf{c} - q(\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{b}) ||_1 \\
    &\leq || \mathbf{c}-q(\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{u}) ||_1 + q|| \mathbf{u}-\mathbf{b} ||_1 & & \\
    &\leq E + q(\lambda-1) & & (\text{Lemmas } \ref{lem:E_ineq}, \; \ref{lem:choose_b}) \\
    &= (n-2)(q-1) - q(\lambda-1) - \Delta + q(\lambda-1) & & (\text{Lemma } \ref{lem:descr_E}) \\
    &\leq (n-2)(q-1) -1 & & (\text{Lemma } \ref{lem:descr_E}) \\
    &= r_q.
\end{align*}
We compute
\begin{align*}
    \varepsilon_i 
    &= c_i-q-qb_i & & \\
    &= (qu_i+q+\rho_i-\eta_i) -q-qb_i & & (\text{Lemma \ref{lem:E_ineq}}) \\
    &\geq q(u_i - b_i) + \rho_i +1 - q & & (\text{Lemma } \ref{lem:E_ineq}(1)) \\
    &\geq 1-q.
\end{align*}
By Lemma \ref{lem:equiv_char}, it follows that $\mathbf{c} \in \mathscr{B}_q$, which proves the reverse containment.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
